structure.overview: This case concerns an appeal by Finastra International Limited against the Canadian trademark registrations of Fenestrae B.V., a Dutch software company, regarding the use and registration of the FENESTRAE mark for various software goods and services. The Federal Court reviewed the evidence of use of the mark in Canada, partially upholding the trademark registrations related to Faxination software and services but finding insufficient evidence for Udocx services. The appeal was allowed in part, with some deletions of goods and services from the registrations, and no costs were awarded due to the divided outcome.

sections.label: Tribunal Below's Findings on Trademark Use and Registrations
Standard of Review and Burden of Proof
Analysis of Evidence for Goods and Sales in Canada
Analysis of Evidence for Services and Use of Udocx Mark

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondent Fenestrae BV is a Dutch software company owning the FENESTRAE mark, with a subsidiary in Georgia providing global support and sales.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondent uses the FENESTRAE mark mainly for Faxination, a secure digital document platform, and Udocx, a cloud-based document conversion solution.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer grouped registered goods and services into Faxination, Udocx, and others, upholding only some registrations; Appellant wants all deleted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The appeal is allowed in part for reasons explained below.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Mr. Hogewoning admitted the mark was unused in Canada for some hardware goods, which were deleted accordingly.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Faxination was described broadly but established as at least computer facsimile software with modular components.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer divided goods into Computer Facsimile Software and Remaining Computer Software Goods.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Computer Facsimile Software included software for transmission and analysis of various media across networks.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: No evidence showed Faxination exchanged audio or moving pictures, so those entries were deleted.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Appellant argued no evidence showed software installation images were viewed in Canada; one document showed a Netherlands account.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found FENESTRAE mark on software installation images sufficient to associate the mark with Faxination subscription.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Remaining Computer Software Goods included backup hard drives, peripherals, mobile devices, and payment processing software.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer agreed backup hard drives lacked sales evidence and deleted those goods accordingly.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Mr. Hogewoning's description of backup hard drives was unsupported by affidavit evidence, so association was rejected.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: No evidence supported payment processing software goods; general references were deleted.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found Faxination descriptions correlated to various telecommunication and facsimile messaging services.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Audio and moving pictures were not described for Faxination and were deleted from registered services.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found Faxination subscription included performance of Faxination services, supported by promotional brochures.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Udocx described as cloud solution converting documents; correlated to user access and cloud computing services.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Despite no Udocx subscriptions, Officer accepted services were advertised and available in Canada during relevant period.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Brochures showed FENESTRAE and UDOCX as distinct marks, each with its own ® symbol.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer did not infer Udocx backorders meant availability but accepted direct sales and website display as evidence of use.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Remaining Solutions not addressed in affidavit were deleted by Officer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Questions of fact and mixed fact-law are reviewed for palpable and overriding error; questions of law for correctness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Interpretation of evidence is reviewed for palpable and overriding error, meaning obvious error affecting outcome.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court must decide if Officer made palpable and overriding errors in inferences from evidence including affidavit and exhibits.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Adverse inference not justified as Respondent does not contest factual deficiencies found by Officer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer found Respondent's evidence sufficient; Appellant bears burden to show palpable and overriding error; no adverse inference.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Appellant argues invoices with Canadian addresses lack shipping costs and no evidence goods arrived in Canada.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Sales qualify as normal trade if genuine arm's length transactions; burden is low and may be inferred by Officer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Justice Nadon in JC Penney explained that a single sale can prove trademark use if in the normal course of trade, excluding token or related-party sales.
idea_list: definition of normal course of trade

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No evidence suggested Mr. Hogewoning's transactions were outside the normal course of trade; the Officer properly relied on documents and explanations.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Nothing indicated the sales in Exhibit D were not genuine commercial transactions or excluded types; Respondent needed only to show genuine sales pattern.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondent needed only a prima facie case; Officer could reasonably infer delivery from invoices with major clients.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer's inferences were based on holistic evidence linking invoices and product descriptions to the trademarked goods.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer accepted Mr. Hogewoning's statement that installation screen was viewed in Canada; no reason to think it differed from Netherlands version.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer found Respondent demonstrated use of Faxination goods, deleting unproven goods; Appellant failed to show palpable error.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Appellant argues invoices don't prove registered services were performed in Canada; ordering services isn't use under s 4(2).

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Services term is liberally construed; performance means Canadians derived tangible benefit during relevant period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer found Faxination services performed and Udocx services at least advertised and available in Canada during relevant period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer reasonably inferred Faxination services performed from evidence including annual subscriptions and invoices to agencies.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Appellant notes Udocx licenses were backordered on PC Canada website, suggesting services weren't available during relevant period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer rejected Appellant's 'tacit admission' claim, accepting Mr. Hogewoning's explanation about sales channels and timing.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No evidence beyond Mr. Hogewoning's assertion showed Udocx use in Canada; mere assertion insufficient per Plough case.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Under s 45, burden is light but evidence must show use within three years, not just bald assertions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondent needed factual assertions showing use; Officer accepted bald assertion and found only advertising and availability.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer erred palpably and overridingly by finding Udocx services used during relevant period without sufficient evidence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Because the appeal's success is divided, no order as to costs will be made.
